about.dates: This report covers your session on Tuesday 20 October 2026 and was prepared on 20 October 2026. If a session is re-analysed, the report is prepared again and carries the new date.
about.footnote: Measured and prepared with PinPoint Studio. Swing images show only the golfer; video stays in the studio.
about.measured: 7 swings with an 8 iron, filmed down-the-line and face-on at high frame rate, with every ball measured by a GC Quad. Your body positions are read from the video by pose tracking; the club and ball numbers come from the launch monitor.
about.notChecked: Some things could not be checked on every swing. How fast the club was moving at its peak: our cameras could see it, but not well enough to judge (7 of 7 swings). Hip movement toward the ball by impact, minus meaning away from it: we had no reliable way to turn the picture into real distances (5 of 7 swings). When your chest turned fastest: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (4 of 7 swings). When your hips turned fastest: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (1 of 7 swings). Four more are listed in the technical appendix. Nothing in this report depends on them.
about.ranges: Each habit is judged against a target range. Most ranges are coaching judgement, set from what good ball-strikers do; a few come from published measurements. They are not fitted to you. A swing outside the range is not a mistake in itself — it is where the evidence points. “Ruled out” on a work-on page means measured, and fine, on these swings with these cameras — not gone for good.

rows.title: Ruled out — measured, and fine

workOns.check: Film from down the line at address. A line straight down from your shoulders should pass close to the balls of your feet rather than out over your toes, and you should be able to lift your toes inside your shoes.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Weight on the toes at address, or “leaning onto the toes at address”.
workOns.cue: Feel your weight settle back toward your shoelaces, so your heels press into the ground as firmly as the balls of your feet.

drills.equipment: a mirror or a phone on a stand, optional
drills.instruction: Stand tall holding the club out in front of you at chest height. Push your hips back and tip your chest forward until the club touches the ground, then let your knees soften. Let your arms hang straight down from your shoulders, and step in or out until the club sits behind the ball with about a hand's width between your hands and your thighs. Rehearse it five times before each practice session.
drills.label: Hinge and let the arms hang
drills.note: If you cannot hinge from the hips without your knees bending a lot or your back rounding, tight hamstrings may be setting the limit, and that is worth a physical check before more repetitions.
drills.targets: To set your posture, knee flex, balance and distance from the ball in one repeatable routine, rather than finding them by feel each time.

workOns.target: How far toward your toes your weight sits at address: 65% foot length or less, on most swings. Today: 76% foot length.
workOns.why: Weight on the toes tips you toward the ball as you swing, so contact drifts toward the heel.

workOns.check: Film face-on at address. With an iron your heels should sit roughly under your shoulders, and only a little wider with the driver.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Stance too wide.
workOns.cue: Feel your heels sit about under your shoulders, in a stance you could turn in freely, a little wider with the driver.

drills.instruction: Lay one stick along your toe line and a second across it, pointing at the ball. Let a club hang from each shoulder to see where your heels should sit, then set up so the crossing stick sits where this club's ball belongs: just inside your lead heel for the driver, moving toward the middle of your stance as the clubs get shorter.
drills.label: Stance and ball-position sticks
drills.note: The right width and position vary a little from golfer to golfer. If a narrower or wider stance is the only way you can turn or keep your balance, that is a question for your coach, not something to force.
drills.targets: To make stance width and ball position the same every time, so that a change in strike comes from the swing and not from the setup.

workOns.check: Film from down the line at address: a line down from your shoulders should pass over your knees and the balls of your feet.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Poor posture at address, or “poor posture”, “bad posture at address”.
workOns.cue: Hinge from your hips until your arms hang straight down, then soften your knees just enough to feel ready.

drills.equipment: a mirror or a phone on a stand, optional
drills.instruction: Stand tall holding the club out in front of you at chest height. Push your hips back and tip your chest forward until the club touches the ground, then let your knees soften. Let your arms hang straight down from your shoulders, and step in or out until the club sits behind the ball with about a hand's width between your hands and your thighs. Rehearse it five times before each practice session.
drills.label: Hinge and let the arms hang
drills.note: If you cannot hinge from the hips without your knees bending a lot or your back rounding, tight hamstrings may be setting the limit, and that is worth a physical check before more repetitions.
drills.targets: To set your posture, knee flex, balance and distance from the ball in one repeatable routine, rather than finding them by feel each time.

workOns.name: Poor posture at address
workOns.saw: Your posture at address is hard to swing from — on all 7 swings, no change from first swing to last.
workOns.why: A posture that is hard to hold changes during the swing, so the strike gets harder to repeat.

workOns.also: “sitting into the lead knee going back”, “lead knee collapses going back”
workOns.cameWith: It came with your head dips going back (5 of the 7 swings we could see). That fits the coaching model, though showing up together is not proof that one causes the other.

workOns.check: Film from down the line and pause at address and at the top. At the top your lead knee should be bent only a little more than at address, and still above the laces of your lead shoe.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Lead knee folds going back, or “sitting into the lead knee going back”, “lead knee collapses going back”.
workOns.cue: Feel your trail hip turn behind you while your lead knee keeps about the bend it had at address.

drills.equipment: a mirror or a phone on a stand
drills.instruction: Cross your arms on your chest and take your posture side-on to a mirror, or with a phone filming from down the line. Turn slowly to the top, letting your trail hip turn behind you, and stop. Check that your lead knee is bent only a little more than at address and is still above the laces of your lead shoe. Hold for two seconds, turn back, and repeat ten times. Then hit easy half shots with the same feel.
drills.label: Steady lead knee turns
drills.note: Good players let the lead knee bend a little going back, so the aim is a little, not none. If your hips will only turn when the knee folds, ask your coach to check how freely your hips turn.
drills.targets: To feel your hips turn going back while your lead leg keeps about the bend it had at address.

drills.equipment: a wall, a cushion or a folded towel
drills.instruction: Take your posture facing a wall, with your forehead resting lightly against a cushion or folded towel on it. With your arms crossed on your chest, make slow backswing turns. Your head should stay touching the cushion, without pressing into it, sliding along it or lifting off it.
drills.label: Head against the wall
drills.note: A little head movement is normal in a good swing, and this drill exaggerates stillness on purpose. If your body will only turn when your head moves, ask your coach to check how freely your upper back and hips turn.
drills.targets: To feel your chest and hips turn while your head stays at its height and in its place.

workOns.goal: Keep your lead knee steady going back
workOns.kicker: Work-on 4 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  7 of 7 swings
workOns.name: Lead knee folds going back
workOns.saw: Your lead knee folds going back — on all 7 swings, easing as the session went on. Typical lead-knee bend added by the top: 36°, against a target of 27° or less; this is a clear miss: well past the range on 5 of 7 swings.
workOns.target: Lead-knee bend added by the top: 27° or less, on most swings. Today: 36°.
workOns.why: When your lead knee folds going back your head drops with it, so you have to come back up in time to strike the ball.

workOns.check: Film face-on with a stick standing upright beside your head at address. At the top your head should have moved away from the target by no more than a ball's width or so.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Head sways off the ball, or “swaying off it”, “off the ball”.
workOns.cue: Let your head turn with you but stay well inside your trail foot, while your chest turns behind the ball.

drills.equipment: a wall, a cushion or a folded towel
drills.instruction: Take your posture facing a wall, with your forehead resting lightly against a cushion or folded towel on it. With your arms crossed on your chest, make slow backswing turns. Your head should stay touching the cushion, without pressing into it, sliding along it or lifting off it.
drills.label: Head against the wall
drills.note: A little head movement is normal in a good swing, and this drill exaggerates stillness on purpose. If your body will only turn when your head moves, ask your coach to check how freely your upper back and hips turn.
drills.targets: To feel your chest and hips turn while your head stays at its height and in its place.

drills.equipment: an alignment stick outside the trail hip, optional
drills.instruction: Take your address position, make a slow backswing turn, and stop at the top. Feel the pressure in the trail hip socket rather than on the outside of the trail foot. Hold for three seconds, then return.
drills.label: Trail hip load and hold
drills.note: The stick is a feedback aid, not the drill. If the hip cannot rotate internally, the slide is the body finding the only route it has.
drills.targets: To feel the trail hip accepting the turn instead of the pelvis sliding away from the target.

workOns.target: Head movement away from the target by the top, minus meaning toward it: 10 cm or less, on most swings. Today: 10.7 cm.
workOns.why: When your head sways away, the bottom of your swing moves with it and contact gets harder to repeat.
